title: The six-tusked elephant
hookLine: an elephant helps the hunter who wounded him cut his tusks (Jataka 514)

cards: The arrow comes from below. An elephant king walks a forest path, and a hunter hidden in a pit shoots a poisoned arrow up into him. In the Jataka this elephant is Chaddanta, the six-tusked, leader of a great herd.
The story could end with him crushing the man in the pit. He has the strength to do it. It doesn't end that way.

teach.b: It started small. Chaddanta had two wives, and one of them, Culla-subhadda, came to believe he favored the other. The slight, the story makes clear, was a shower of blossoms that fell on the wrong wife.
She nursed it until she died wishing for revenge, and was reborn as a queen in a human kingdom. As queen, she sent a hunter named Sonuttara to find the elephant and bring back his tusks.

teach.h: A HUNTER IN A YELLOW ROBE.
teach.b: He made the long journey and hid in a pit, wearing the yellow robe of a renunciant. Then the turn. Wounded, Chaddanta went for him, saw the robe, and stopped.

He would not harm someone wearing that cloth, even as a trick. He asked the hunter why, heard about the queen, and understood who wanted him dead. The hunter tried to saw off the tusks and couldn't manage it.

teach.h: THE SAW IN HIS OWN TRUNK.
teach.b: So Chaddanta took the saw in his own trunk, cut the tusks himself, handed them over, and died. Notice what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the wound didn't matter.

It doesn't call the hunter good. It shows someone who had every right to strike back, and chose to help instead. When the queen saw the tusks, the story says, she remembered who he had been, and grief overwhelmed her.
The grudge ran the whole story. The elephant is the one who stopped it.

how: Buddhist teachers retell the Chaddanta story as a tale of patience and forgiveness; Buddhists practice letting go of resentment through reflection and loving-kindness meditation.

o: a hunter who hid in a forest pit
a queen who nursed an old grudge

games.q: who's who in the elephant's story: tap the pairs.
p: the wife who nursed a grudge
the hunter in the yellow robe

s: the elephant crushed the hunter in the pit
he stopped when he saw the robe, and later cut his own tusks for the hunter.
the hunter hid wearing a renunciant's yellow robe
Chaddanta would not harm someone in that cloth, even worn as a disguise.
the trouble began with a slight over blossoms
one wife came to believe he favored the other, and carried the grudge into her next life.

games.q: you're Chaddanta, wounded by a hunter in a pit. you see he's wearing a renunciant's robe. what do you do?
o: crush him anyway; he shot you.
stop, and ask him why he did it.
turn away into the forest and leave him.
games.why: he stops at the sight of the robe and asks why; when the hunter can't cut the tusks, the elephant cuts them for him.

practice: Bring to mind a small hurt, not the biggest one you carry: a sharp word, someone who took the credit.

Find where it sits in the body, the jaw, the chest, the stomach, and without calling it fine, try setting it down for one breath, the way the elephant stopped at the sight of a robe. If it comes back, set it down again.

wordCard.voice: Chaddanta. The six-tusked elephant king who, wounded by a hunter, helped him take the tusks he came for. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Chaddanta, the elephant's name, given in English as six-tusked.

carryVoice: Your line: he helped the hunter. He had every right to strike back. Day eight hundred thirty-eight, done.
